title: As Exotics Go, the Maserati Bora Still Makes Sense

body_markdown:
Until the recent debut of the[12Cilindri Manuale](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/cammisa-ferraris-12cilindri-manuale-is-the-real-deal/) , Ferrari’s answer to anyone asking for a new manual supercar was wonderfully Ferrari: Buy an old one. It’s not the only Italian luxury automaker to perform such an about-face: Maserati is headed in that direction, too. Cristiano Fiorio, the company’s marketing head and director of its bespoke tailoring program BottegaFuoriserie, says around half the program’s clients want gas power and a manual gearbox, and that[a future limited-run flagship](https://www.magnetomagazine.com/articles/maserati-updates-range-and-commits-to-manual-hypercar-and-new-quattroporte/) will need both.


To which we say: Good. Maserati has form here. Fifty-five years ago, the Bora showed that a mid-engined supercar could be fast, civilized, and manual, without requiring its owner to travel everywhere with an osteopath.


The Bora came from a moment when Maserati had little choice but to change. Citroën took control in 1968, bringing money, engineering confidence, and an enthusiasm for high-pressure hydraulics. Meanwhile, the Lamborghini Miura had moved the engine behind the seats and made every traditional front-engined GT look as contemporary as a hot dog cart in Central Park.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Development of Tipo 117 began in 1968 under Giulio Alfieri, but the point was not simply to copy the Miura. This had to remain a proper Maserati—rapid enough to trouble the new mid-engined exotica but refined enough for the marque’s GT clientele. It needed luggage space, tolerable noise levels, and the ability to deliver you to your destination without looking as though you had been stored beside the exhaust manifolds. The finished Maserati Bora appeared at Geneva in March 1971. Ferrari unveiled the 365 GT4 BB later that year, but production did not begin until 1973.


Giorgetto Giugiaro had drawn the Bora for Italdesign, resisting the temptation to garnish it with every wedge-era styling trick available. The form is clean: a low nose, one rising waistline, a compact greenhouse, and a chopped tail. At just under 45 inches high, it looks dramatic without appearing to have been flattened by industrial equipment.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


The brushed stainless-steel roof and windscreen pillars do much of the visual heavy lifting. They divide the body from the greenhouse and make the cabin resemble the lid of an expensive 1970s stereo. Pop-up headlamps keep the nose unspoiled, while the glazed rear bodywork displays the V-8 without making the occupants smell it.


Officine Padane built the all-steel body in Modena. Beneath the rear glass sat a removable, carpeted aluminum inner engine cover, to isolate heat and mechanical noise. The Bora looked exotic, but it was designed by people who understood that owners might occasionally travel somewhere.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Inside, Giugiaro avoided the traditional Italian arrangement of placing the pedals near Florence while leaving the steering wheel in Turin. The seat adjusted back and forth for height, the steering column moved for reach and rake, and Citroën hydraulics shifted the seat up and down. There were electric windows, leather trim, a useful front trunk, and optional air conditioning. Double glazing separated the cabin from the engine bay.


Underneath was a steel monocoque with the engine, five-speed ZF transaxle, and rear suspension carried on a detachable subframe. Flexible mountings reduced vibration. Double wishbones, coil springs, telescopic dampers, and anti-roll bars appeared at each corner, making the Bora Maserati’s first road car with fully independent suspension.


Then there were the hydraulics. They powered the ventilated disc brakes, raised the headlamps, altered the pedal position, and adjusted the driver’s seat height. The brake pedal has almost no travel, making the first stop feel as though someone has dropped an anchor through the floor. Familiarity helps. So does not approaching a roundabout in unfamiliar loafers.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


The original 4.7-liter, four-cam V-8 produced 310 horsepower and around 340 lb-ft, fed by four twin-choke Weber carburetors. *Autocar* magazine recorded 0–60 mph in 6.5 seconds, 100 mph in 15.3 seconds, and 162 mph flat out. The later European 4.9 was quoted at around 325 hp and up to 355 lb-ft, while emissions-controlled American cars produced less. Maserati claimed 177 mph for the strongest 4.9, though that remains a factory figure.


Numbers only explain half of it, though. The V-8 is less frantic than a Ferrari flat-12 and less operatic than a Miura’s V-12, but it has the low-rev shove that makes overtaking a breeze—which is where its name comes from (a wind from the Trieste region). The unassisted steering was praised in period for being precise and surprisingly light, even at parking speeds. Squeezing into spots was awkward, though, because rearward visibility was less than great.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


*Motor Sport* called the Bora one of the world’s best road sports cars, praising roadholding and handling that had few equals away from a circuit. It also recorded the less glamorous details: a heavy clutch, a sprung and occasionally notchy gearshift, a cramped passenger footwell, sensitive wet-weather braking, and faults on the test car. Nevertheless, at pace the Bora became stable, balanced, and effective rather than theatrical for its own sake; a supercar for adults, then.


Its commercial life was more of a struggle. The oil crisis arrived, Citroën’s financial troubles pushed Maserati into liquidation, and Alejandro de Tomaso took control in 1975. Bora production continued until 1978, by which time Maserati had built 564 of them, against 387 Ferrari 365 GT4 BBs.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Perhaps unsurprisingly, the market still favors the Ferrari heavily, with #2 (excellent) examples of the 365 GT4 BB in the neighborhood of[a half-million bucks](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/365_gt4_bb/1974/1974-ferrari-365_gt4_bb-base?id=aCn1I000000DSgbSAG&condition=excellent) . Meanwhile, average auction values for a Bora 4.7 in similar condition hover between $115K and $140K, with #3 (good) drivers around $100K and #1 (concours) cars somewhere between $155K and $195K. The 4.9-liter cars carry[a slight premium](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/maserati/bora/1972/1972-maserati-bora-4.9l?id=aCn1I000000D4A9SAK&condition=excellent) , with #3 examples valued around $20K more overall, #2 cars about $25K higher, and #1 examples generally $30K higher. Sales in the last 12 months have included everything from[a non-running 1977 4.9L project](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1977-maserati-bora-6/) in Belgium for $53K to[a 1978 4.9 with a recent refurbishment](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1978-maserati-bora/) for $182,500.[The car pictured here](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/past-sales/1972-maserati-bora/AM117120/7dbdc9fa-72e3-40c8-baf9-229d1bab4441) , a ’72 with the 4.7-liter engine, sold in April at Broad Arrow’s Amelia Concours Auction for $128,800. On the ground, Hagerty auction analysts rated it in #3+ condition, with the following assessment: *Restoration work performed in the 2010s but never fully taken apart and redone. Decent paint with a crack ahead of the engine cover, and bits of paint coming up around the door handles. Surface rust on the radio antenna and exhaust tips. Imperfect panel fit. Good, lightly worn interior. Clean, maintained chassis and engine. Attractive color on an inherently attractive car, in better-than-average driver condition.*


Do not simply buy the cheapest one you can find, of course. Corrosion, tired cooling systems, poor wiring, and neglect can turn a bargain Bora into a second mortgage with Campagnolo wheels. The hydraulics are not inherently disastrous, but they need correct LHM fluid, healthy accumulators, and somebody who knows Citroën systems rather than merely fears them. Buy history, condition, and specialist knowledge before engine size.


Even at top money, the Bora looks like an oddly good value beside a comparable Berlinetta Boxer. It is more comfortable, more discreet, and no less capable of making everyone else at the gas station stop dead in their tracks. Ferrari says manual enthusiasts should look backwards (or wait for a call for eligibility to buy their 12Cilindri). Fine. Maserati’s past shows exactly why its future manual flagship makes sense.
